options: Nothing is wrong; both handlers will run
`Exception` catches everything first, so `ValueError` is never reached
`ValueError` must come before all other exceptions
You cannot have more than one `except` clause
questions.explanation: Python checks `except` clauses in order. Since `Exception` is a base class that catches all exceptions, the `ValueError` clause is unreachable. Specific exceptions must always come before general ones.

questions.question: What does the `finally` block do?
options: Runs only if no exception occurred
Runs only if an exception occurred
Always runs, whether or not an exception occurred
Re-raises the exception to the caller
questions.explanation: `finally` always executes—after try, after except, and even after a `return` statement. It is designed for cleanup code (closing files, releasing locks) that must run regardless of what happened.

questions.question: When does the `else` clause in a try-except block run?
options: When an exception is caught by an `except` clause
When no exception occurred in the `try` block
Always, before `finally`
Only when a `ValueError` is raised
questions.explanation: The `else` clause runs only when the `try` block completes without raising any exception. It is useful for code that should execute only on success, separate from the cleanup in `finally`.

questions.question: How do you catch an exception and re-raise it after logging?
options: `except Error: raise Error()`
`except Error as e: raise e.again()`
`except Error as e: logger.error(e); raise`
`except Error: continue`
questions.explanation: A bare `raise` inside an `except` block re-raises the currently handled exception unchanged. This lets you log the error for observability while still propagating the exception to the caller.

questions.question: What is the correct way to define a custom exception class?
options: `class MyError: pass`
`class MyError(Exception): pass`
`class MyError extends Exception: pass`
`def MyError(Exception): pass`
questions.explanation: Custom exceptions must inherit from `Exception` (or a subclass). This ensures they work with all standard exception-handling mechanisms like `try/except`, `raise`, and `isinstance()` checks.
